USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Go into the G20 Osaka meeting and secure a truce — resume the suspended talks, hold off on the threatened $300B tariff list, and trade the easing of Huawei/entity-list measures for verifiable Chinese commitments on IP, technology transfer, and purchases. Do not escalate further this week; use the leader-to-leader channel to stop the escalation spiral before it hits US consumer goods and tips expectations into recession. Keep the structural-reform endgame intact as the prize of a real deal.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is real but not existential (+0.35). The US initiated and still holds leverage, so this is far from the +1.0 existential anchor, but the costs of the dispute are now visibly mounting: the 10-year Treasury yield has collapsed from ~2.7% in January to ~2.0% and the 2-year to ~1.77% by late June (country_health DGS10/DGS2), with the dollar softening and the market pricing in Fed cuts — clear signs investors view the trade war as a growth/recession risk. The farm belt is already bleeding: China's soybean retaliation cost farmers ~$7.9B, with ~27.5M tons expected unsold and a $16B bailout needed (web: Business Insider/USDA); this is a direct hit to the administration's political base ahead of 2020. Escalation risk is real — the threatened $300B list would tax everyday US consumer electronics (timeline 2019-05-05; Guardian), and the Huawei/entity-list + unreliable-entity-list exchange (timeline 2019-05-16, 2019-05-31) risks fragmenting global tech supply chains that US firms depend on. Given all this, the right stance is moderate de-escalation via negotiation (+0.2): the June 18 Trump-Xi phone call and agreed Osaka meeting (timeline 2019-06-18) have reopened a channel; squeezing a truce now — resume talks and pause further escalation — protects US growth and farm interests without surrendering the US bargaining position on structural change and enforcement.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Attend the G20 Osaka meeting and use it to restart official trade negotiations with the United States, without committing to new structural concessions up front. Seek a reprieve/cooling on the threatened additional $300B in tariffs and a path to roll back the Huawei entity list, while publicly positioning China as the side open to equal, mutually beneficial talks. Hold the current tariff posture rather than escalating with rare-earth or other countermeasures, which would only deepen the conflict and harm our standing as a defender of the multilateral trading order.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high, not existential. The US has imposed 25% tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese goods and explicitly threatened to extend tariffs to essentially all remaining imports (~$300B, including consumer electronics) if the Osaka meeting yields no progress (timeline 2019-05-05/05-10; Reuters 2019-06-26). Firm-level targeting has intensified with Huawei's Entity List placement, Google suspending Android/GMS access, and US chip suppliers pausing sales (timeline 2019-05-15/05-16/05-20) — squarely the CHN +0.5 firm-targeting/export-sector anchor, arguably higher given the tech-decoupling dimension. Macro evidence corroborates a real toll: China's export growth decelerated sharply (December 2018 exports -4% y/y vs +11% in April 2018), the Shanghai Composite fell ~16% over the year, and trade-war feedback loops have slowed growth independently of official GDP prints (HedgeNordic, Mar 2019); China has eased via RRR cuts while guarding the currency. These justify a +0.55 threat score: major export hubs and a national champion are hit and the escalation path is live, but reserves (~$3T), policy room, and the imminent G20 off-ramp keep it short of existential. On action: Washington itself seeks to restart talks at Osaka and even floated a possible no-new-tariffs goodwill gesture (Reuters 2019-06-26), while expectations are deliberately low — the realistic best case is a resumption of official negotiations, taking months. Given that a genuine meeting is now on the table (Trump-Xi call, June 18), the rational stance is to negotiate and hold our line rather than escalate: escalating via rare-earth or reserve actions would risk the global economy, alienate allies, and hand the US rhetorical ammunition. Conceding structural reforms before talks resume would forfeit leverage. Hence negotiate (action_score 0.0) — engage, buy time, and keep all escalatory options in reserve.
